clue.text: The usual range of eating-out places

definitions.text: The usual range of eating-out places

parts.words: The usual range of eating-out places
parts.note: a 'range' is a cooking stove, and 'eating-out' is read literally as eating outdoors, so this is the grill used for meals in the garden

explanation.surface: A guide describing the typical choice of restaurants in town.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor grill is the cooking range people use when they eat in the open air.

clue.text: Main case involved The Man Who Forgot

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters of main case are jumbled together

explanation.surface: The chief legal case concerned a film or book called The Man Who Forgot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' looks like 'concerned', but it signals that MAIN CASE is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone suffering memory loss is a person who forgets, like the title character.

clue.text: Order soldiers to become more violent initially to cause confusion

indicators.note: order here tells the solver to arrange the pieces in a different sequence from the clue's

parts.note: become gives the verb be
wilder means fiercer, more violent
men is a common word for soldiers, as in officers and men

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the word to is taken

explanation.surface: A commander orders his troops to grow fiercer so as to sow confusion among the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' reads as a command to the troops, but it tells the solver to put the soldiers after the violence; 'initially' takes the first letter of 'to', and 'to cause' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bewilderment is a state of being perplexed and baffled, a synonym of confusion.

clue.text: Curve in line 'concealing heavy artillery of old

indicators.note: concealing means the letters are disguised, so curve in plus the line letter are rearranged to hide the answer

explanation.surface: A bend in a defensive line hides big old guns from the enemy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealing' is a loose anagram signal: CURVE IN plus L (line) are disguised by rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A culverin was a long cannon of the 16th and 17th centuries, an old piece of heavy ordnance.

clue.text: Parts of Valence where one is surrounded by strangers

definitions.text: where one is surrounded by strangers

indicators.note: parts of suggests the word Valence is broken into pieces and reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: Somewhere in the French town of Valence a person feels hemmed in by foreigners.
explanation.walkthrough: Valence is a town in France; 'Parts of' asks for its letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclave is a territory wholly surrounded by foreign land, so its people are ringed by outsiders.

clue.text: City that was great, say, when Cobbett described it

definitions.text: City that was great, say, when Cobbett described it

parts.words: City that was great, say, when Cobbett described it
parts.note: the radical writer William Cobbett famously called the British capital 'the Great Wen', a wen being a swollen cyst

explanation.surface: A historical note on a city that was magnificent in Cobbett's day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great' seems to mean splendid, but it echoes Cobbett's phrase 'the Great Wen', his insulting name for the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobbett's nickname 'the Great Wen' referred to the capital of England, which he saw as a bloated growth.

clue.text: The way round a covered walk

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: Follow the path that circles a sheltered colonnade.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue drops 'a'; the printed page has it. A stoa was a covered colonnade in ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoa was a roofed portico in Greek architecture where people strolled, a sheltered promenade.

clue.text: Old vehicle in which two appeared on the box

definitions.meaning: a four-wheeled closed horse-drawn carriage of the 19th century

definitions.text: in which two appeared on the box
definitions.meaning: the cross-eyed lion in the television series Daktari saw everything double

explanation.surface: A vintage carriage in which a pair of people featured on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two appeared' is the lion's double vision: Clarence the Cross-Eyed Lion saw two of everything on screen ('the box' is TV).
explanation.definitionFit: A clarence was a carriage named after the Duke of Clarence; the TV lion of Daktari bore the same name.

clue.text: One turbulent part of S Africa of recent origin

indicators.note: turbulent means disturbed, so the letters of one are stirred up

parts.note: Natal was a province of South Africa

explanation.surface: A troubled region in the south of the continent has only just come into being.
explanation.walkthrough: The held clue misreads 'S Africa' as 'Africa'. ONE scrambled gives NEO, then NATAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Neonatal describes a newborn, something that has only just begun life.

clue.text: Identified unusual sound

indicators.note: sound tells us the word is heard rather than read, so a word with the same pronunciation is wanted

parts.note: something unusual is new, novel

explanation.surface: An odd noise was recognised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like the noun being identified, but it is the signal that NEW is to be heard.
explanation.definitionFit: To have recognised someone is to have known who they were.

clue.text: Its occupant is not fit for the Bath professorship

definitions.text: Its occupant is not fit for the Bath professorship

parts.words: Its occupant is not fit for the Bath professorship
parts.note: a 'chair' looks like an academic post at Bath university, but it is a Bath chair whose occupant is unwell, not physically fit

explanation.surface: A remark that the holder of a university post at Bath is unsuitable for it.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bath chair was a hooded wheeled chair for the sick, named after the spa town; 'professorship' tempts towards an academic chair.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bath chair is a wheeled seat for a sick person, whose occupant is unwell.

clue.text: Dessert in quick food establishment?

parts.note: read literally, a quickly made pudding; it is also the name of a famous Harvard student club

explanation.surface: Asking about the sweet course at a fast-food outlet.
explanation.walkthrough: A hasty pudding is a quick porridge-like dish of flour or oatmeal boiled in milk; the Hasty Pudding Club at Harvard is the 'establishment'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish of flour or oats stirred in boiling milk is a quick sweet course.

clue.text: A burnt-out case on the track?

definitions.text: A burnt-out case on the track?

parts.words: A burnt-out case on the track?
parts.note: a 'burnt-out case' suggests an exhausted athlete, but it is a scrap of burnt coal used to surface running tracks

explanation.surface: An exhausted runner on the athletics track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A Burnt-Out Case' is a Graham Greene novel; here it is literal: a burnt fragment of coal, laid on old running tracks.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece of coal that has burnt out was used to surface athletics tracks.

clue.text: Sun naive enough to produce one from outer space?

indicators.note: to produce asks for something new to be made from the letters of sun naive by rearranging them

explanation.surface: The Sun newspaper is gullible enough to report an alien visitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' is italicised as the newspaper, but it is simply fodder with NAIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A being from the planet named after the goddess of love would be an alien.

clue.text: Where sessions sometimes take place unexpectedly

definitions.text: Where sessions sometimes take place unexpectedly

parts.words: Where sessions sometimes take place unexpectedly
parts.note: a skating session where people unexpectedly 'take place', that is sit down hard on the ice after a fall

explanation.surface: A remark about meetings that happen without warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sessions' suggests meetings, but 'sessions ... take place' hides sit-downs: falls on the frozen surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A rink for skating is where skaters sometimes fall and land sitting down.

clue.text: Brood in a rage about copper

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the phrase for in a rage goes round the copper symbol

parts.note: 'in a bate' is British slang for in a temper
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: Someone sulks furiously about a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the element. 'In a bate' is old British slang for being angry.
explanation.definitionFit: To brood is to sit on eggs to hatch them, keeping them warm until they develop.

clue.text: Gilbert's dream 'transport for crossing the Plain

definitions.text: Gilbert's dream 'transport for crossing the Plain

parts.words: Gilbert's dream 'transport for crossing the Plain
parts.note: in W S Gilbert's Nightmare Song from Iolanthe the dreamer is crossing Salisbury Plain on a two-wheeled machine

explanation.surface: W S Gilbert's ideal vehicle for getting over Salisbury Plain.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Lord Chancellor's Nightmare Song (Iolanthe, Gilbert and Sullivan) the dreamer crosses Salisbury Plain, a large open area in southern England, by pedal power.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-wheeled pedal machine was the vehicle in the nightmare song's journey.

clue.text: Here's a trespasser to push in the river!

parts.note: to intrude is to push in where one is not wanted
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An order to shove a prowler into the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'push in the river' reads as a threat, but it splits as 'push in' plus R.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who enters land without permission is one who has pushed in uninvited.

clue.text: He had Mark Twain on his line

definitions.text: He had Mark Twain on his line

parts.words: He had Mark Twain on his line
parts.note: a sailor sounding the depth with a weighted line calls 'mark twain' for two fathoms, which gave the author his pen name

explanation.surface: Someone got the author Mark Twain on the telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark Twain' was the river call for two fathoms, made by the sailor heaving the weighted sounding line.
explanation.definitionFit: The sailor who heaves the sounding weight calls out the depth marked on his line.

clue.text: Invalid food and drink served up with a mild seasoning

parts.note: pap is soft mushy food for invalids or babies

indicators.note: served up in a down clue means the drink is written upwards, so read from the bottom

parts.note: kir is a drink of white wine and blackcurrant liqueur

explanation.surface: A sick person's meal and drink brought with gentle spicing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' turns KIR to RIK in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: This red powder from sweet peppers is a gentle spice.

clue.text: One of the French dame's flowers

definitions.text: One of the French dame's flowers

parts.words: One of the French dame's flowers
parts.note: Dumas's novel La Dame aux Camelias is named after its heroine's favourite blossoms

explanation.surface: A bloom from a Frenchwoman's bouquet.
explanation.walkthrough: La Dame aux Camelias, by Alexandre Dumas fils, is the source of Verdi's La Traviata.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Dumas's novel always wore these glossy-leaved shrub blooms.

clue.text: A deviation 'from the general scheme

parts.note: Robert E Lee was the Confederate general
a way is a method or scheme

explanation.surface: A departure from the overall plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'general scheme' reads as 'overall plan', but 'general' is General Lee.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeway is a ship's sideways drift off course, hence any deviation or latitude.

clue.text: A bird or two can talk

indicators.note: talk signals that the words two can are spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bird, or perhaps a couple of them, is able to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two can talk' looks like a pair of talking birds, but 'talk' signals the sound of 'two can'.
explanation.definitionFit: The big-billed tropical American species is a kind of bird.

clue.text: The area of conflict for William?

definitions.text: The area of conflict for William?

parts.words: The area of conflict for William?
parts.note: William the Conqueror won at Hastings, at the spot where the town of Battle now stands in Sussex

explanation.surface: Asking where William fought.
explanation.walkthrough: The town of Battle in East Sussex grew up on the site of the 1066 Battle of Hastings, so William's patch was literally Battle ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A place where armies fight is a field of conflict.

clue.text: Ram down woolly hat before Cup Final

parts.note: a tam, short for tam-o'-shanter, is a Scottish woollen beret

indicators.note: Final means the last letter of the word Cup is used

explanation.surface: A fan pulls a woolly hat down tight before the Cup Final.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cup Final' reads as a football match, but 'Final' takes the last letter of 'Cup'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack earth or a charge firmly is to pound it down.

clue.text: Girl, single, going to Sandhurst

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one, single
RMA is the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst, the British Army's officer college

explanation.surface: An unmarried young woman goes off to military college.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandhurst is the British Army's officer academy, the RMA.
explanation.definitionFit: Irma is a female forename, so it can stand for a girl.

clue.text: Boy with a tout and a scalper

parts.note: Tom is a boy's name
to hawk is to tout or peddle goods

explanation.surface: A lad with a ticket tout and a black-market seller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scalper' and 'tout' suggest ticket sellers, but the scalper is a weapon used for scalping.
explanation.definitionFit: A Native American war axe was used to take scalps.

clue.text: Too proud to take a grant or other arrangement

indicators.note: other arrangement asks for the letters of a grant or to be put in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone is too haughty to accept a grant or any other deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'other arrangement' looks like an alternative deal, but it signals that A GRANT OR is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Being arrogant means having an overbearing sense of one's own importance, excessively proud.
